overview:
Mountainous, overwhelmingly Armenian-populated, and administratively attached to Soviet Azerbaijan in 1923, Nagorno-Karabakh became the first place where the Soviet Union's national question turned violent. In February 1988 the region's legislature voted to transfer to Armenia; Moscow refused, pogroms against Armenians followed in Sumgait and later Baku, and by 1991 the dispute had become a war between two republics that were themselves becoming independent states. Local Armenian authorities proclaimed a republic in September 1991, held a referendum in December that the Azerbaijani minority boycotted, and formally declared independence on 6 January 1992. The fighting that followed killed roughly 25,000 to 30,000 people and displaced hundreds of thousands on both sides. When a Russian-brokered ceasefire took hold on 12 May 1994, Armenian forces held not only the former autonomous oblast but seven surrounding Azerbaijani districts, from which the Azerbaijani population had fled or been expelled.

For nearly thirty years the entity governed itself with the apparatus of a state — presidents, a National Assembly, an army, a capital at Stepanakert — while no United Nations member, not even Armenia, ever recognised it. It used the Armenian dram, depended on Yerevan for budget subsidies and officers, and connected to the outside world through a single mountain road, the Lachin corridor. Internationally it remained part of Azerbaijan, and the OSCE Minsk Group's mediation, co-chaired by Russia, France and the United States, produced frameworks but no settlement while Azerbaijan's oil revenues rebuilt its army. In 2017 a constitutional referendum renamed it the Republic of Artsakh, after the ancient Armenian province, though the older name stayed in common use.

The end came in three stages. Azerbaijan's forty-four-day offensive in autumn 2020 recovered the occupied districts and part of Karabakh itself, including Shusha, and left the remainder linked to Armenia only by the corridor, now patrolled by Russian peacekeepers. In December 2022 that corridor was closed by Azerbaijani protesters and then by checkpoint; the International Court of Justice ordered Baku in February 2023 to allow unimpeded movement, and the order was not complied with, leaving some 120,000 people short of food, fuel and medicine through the summer. On 19 September 2023 Azerbaijan launched what it called an anti-terrorist operation; the Karabakh authorities capitulated within a day, and in the week that followed virtually the entire Armenian population — over 100,000 people — drove out along the same road to Armenia. On 28 September the last president, Samvel Shahramanyan, signed a decree dissolving all state institutions as of 1 January 2024.
significance: Artsakh was the longest-lived of the post-Soviet unrecognised states, and its disappearance closed the first of the Soviet Union's ethno-territorial wars — the one that began before the USSR itself ended. Its collapse showed how little protection de facto statehood, a binding World Court order, or a great-power patron actually offered: Russia's peacekeepers, distracted by the war in Ukraine, stood by, and the international response to the depopulation of the region was diplomatic rather than material. For Armenians the loss registered as the end of a continuous presence of well over a millennium in the highlands and as a rupture with Moscow that reoriented Armenian foreign policy westward; for Azerbaijan it was the completion of a national project three decades in the making, and the basis for the peace framework the two states have been negotiating since. It also stands as one of the clearest recent cases of a population removed in its entirety in days, and of how quickly a functioning polity of 120,000 people can cease to exist.
coverage: Written from encyclopedic and institutional overviews plus the ICJ case record; the dataset itself holds no events for this story, so nothing here is anchored to a mappable point. Casualty figures for 1991–94 are estimates that vary widely, wartime accounts from both sides are heavily partisan (one chronology used here comes from an Armenian studies institute), and there is no neutral accounting of what happened inside Karabakh during the September 2023 operation or of the legal status of the dissolution decree, which parts of the exiled leadership have since contested.
